These must be handled with caution. The stress pattern in these languages was deduced from old scanty material found in the Australian Institute for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) library and at the Australian National University (ANU).' Code legend at lines 10404-10416: 'E: the descriptive source notes many exceptions to the general rule'. Heading at lines 10880-10881: 'VI Stress is on the second syllable if it is heavy, otherwise on the first:' (this heading sits on p. 246, just before the 'APPENDIX D 247' running head at l…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand database summary: main stress falls on the second syllable when that syllable is heavy (heaviness counting both vowel length and vowel height), otherwise on the first syllable; the compiler flags many exceptions and says the language may instead be lexically unpredictable between initial and second-syllable stress. No primary description is cited; per the appendix preamble the pattern was deduced from unreferenced AIATSIS/ANU manuscript material (presumably Breen's).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated for Wagaya (the type-VI heading says nothing about secondary stress; no RS/ES/NS code given).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Many exceptions' (code E = 'the descriptive source notes many exceptions to the general rule'); 'may also belong in the unpredictable, initial or second category'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress type in a typological database; no domain, citation-form, dialect (Western vs Eastern Wakaya) or data are given.
new_statements.identity_note: Wagaya = Wakaya (community name 'Wuka'), AIATSIS C16, Tindale T247 'Wakaja'. Breen distinguishes Wakaya proper (western; two noun classes; the variety his phonology ms describes as 'the western dialect') from Eastern Wakaya (possibly a koine shared with Yindjilandji yind1248 and Bularnu bula1255); Dixon 2002 treats Yindjilandji as a Wagaya dialect. Goedemans' 'Wagaya (T247)' entry does not say which dialect it reflects. Goedemans lists sister Bularnu (T246) separately under initial stress, so the entry is not a subgroup-level generalisation.
